title: Revive a cloud-dead robot vacuum with a local server
summary: A user had Claude Code reverse-engineer a $400 robot vacuum's link to its shut-down cloud and build a local server; they say it now cleans on schedule again.
agent_role: Claude Code worked out how the vacuum talked to the maker's servers and built a local server to control it. The human set the schedule and ran three checks before leaving it running.
outcome: Author reports the vacuum, unused for two years after the maker's cloud shut down, now cleans at 8:30 every weekday under local control.
what_they_did: The poster's $400 robot vacuum sat in a cupboard for two years after the maker's online service shut down. They used Claude Code to work out how the robot talked to those servers, then build a replacement server on their own computer. Their first request was to clean at 8:30 every weekday at 40% suction and return to the dock.
how_it_went: They say the robot works again, handling navigation itself while their computer runs the server and schedule. They tested it with internet blocked, after a server restart, and with the robot disconnected.
worth_knowing: The computer must stay on to run the server and schedule. The author checked that a restart would not repeat a cleaning job and that lost connections were flagged.
prompt: My [robot vacuum brand and model] stopped working because the maker's cloud service shut down, but the hardware is fine. Help me figure out how it communicates on my home network and build a small local server on my computer to control it. Explain your plan and each step before changing any device settings. Then set a schedule: clean at [time] on [days], use [suction level], and return to the dock when done. Before we finish, help me test that it works with internet blocked, that restarting the server doesn't repeat a job, and that a lost connection is clearly flagged.

curation.rationale: An original home use: reviving abandoned hardware by having Claude Code figure out its cloud protocol and replace it with a local server, with concrete safety checks. Full process is promised but not included, so evidence is the author's account.
